chunks: Design considerations from body diode behavior. The question: What considerations must be taken given the internal body diode behavior?
In a synchronous buck, both transistors are switched off for a few nanoseconds at every hand-over, so they never short the input.
During those gaps the inductor current flows through the bottom transistor's built-in diode instead. That diode has three side effects you must design around.
It wastes some power, it stores charge that causes a spike when it is forced off, and it pulls the switch node below ground.
Picture a crowd forced through a narrow side door while the main door is shut. Every second spent there costs effort.
When the main door reopens, people still in the side door must back out, and that rush causes a brief jam. A shorter wait and a better side door both help.
This is a model with assumed parameters (a 30 nC saturating recovery charge and an exponential shoot-through onset), not measured data.
The shape is the message: loss is high at very short dead time (overlap), drops to a minimum near 20 nanoseconds here, then rises slowly.
Real controllers aim for the left edge of the flat region plus margin, and track it over temperature and load.
Body diode: the diode built into every power MOSFET, which conducts during dead time ("Body diode in the off state, SW waveform").
Dead time: the short gap when both transistors are off ("Shoot-through and dead time"). Switch node: the point between the two transistors that feeds the inductor.
Reverse-recovery charge ( Q rr ): charge stored in the diode that must be swept out before it stops conducting.
Conduction loss: heat from the diode's voltage drop times the current through it. Undershoot: the dip of the switch node below ground.
Take a 2 amps buck switching 500,000 times a second, with a 0. 75 volts body-diode drop.
Each cycle has two hand-overs, with 25 nanoseconds of dead time at each, so the diode conducts 50 nanoseconds per cycle. That is 50 nanoseconds times 500 kilohertz equals 2.
